text.title: Consistency and Standards Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules every Consistency and Standards application MUST enforce, plus a skip-this-methodology fallback. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them. Five consistency types, the prioritization hierarchy, and concrete implementation patterns for visual, functional, and verbal layers.

rule.statement: The audit MUST cover all five layers: internal, external, visual, functional, verbal. Partial-layer audits are rejected. Apply consistency across all five layers: internal (within product), external (with platform/industry), visual (appearance), functional (behavior), and verbal (language).
rule.rationale: Single-layer audits miss the orthogonal failure modes; visual-only audits ignore terminology drift. Addressing only visual consistency while ignoring verbal consistency still forces users to relearn terminology between sections — each layer independently increases cognitive load when violated.

rule.statement: Every audited element MUST carry a numeric variation count. "Many" / "lots" is rejected. Measure consistency by counting distinct style variants for each UI element, not by subjective assessment of whether things "look consistent".
rule.rationale: Numeric counts make the gap measurable and the consolidation outcome verifiable. Subjective assessment is not repeatable and cannot track improvement over time. Counting variants (3 button styles found, target 1) produces a trackable metric.

rule.statement: Consolidation recommendations MUST be ranked by user impact (frequency × visibility × confusion risk). Unranked lists are rejected.
rule.rationale: Unranked lists devolve to "low-hanging fruit first" and miss the high-impact buried-but-rare cases.

rule.statement: External-layer findings MUST cite the platform convention (iOS HIG section, Material spec, WCAG criterion) the product violates.
rule.rationale: Citing the convention makes the recommendation reviewable; uncited claims become opinion.

rule.statement: Every Must-fix finding MUST be paired with a design-system entry (token, component, or pattern). Findings without codification are rejected.
rule.rationale: Without codification the same drift recurs next quarter; the system entry is the durable fix.

rule.statement: When internal and external conventions conflict, always defer to industry conventions first, then platform conventions, then product family conventions.
rule.rationale: Users bring expectations from the wider ecosystem. Violating well-established industry patterns to enforce internal uniqueness always costs more in user confusion than it gains in brand distinctiveness.

rule.statement: Define a single canonical color, size, and spacing value for each semantic role and apply it without exception.
rule.rationale: Even one exception trains designers to treat the system as optional, accelerating drift. The value of a token system is in its 100% adoption.

rule.statement: The same gesture or interaction must produce the same result everywhere in the product without exception.
rule.rationale: If swipe-left deletes in one list but navigates in another, users cannot build a reliable mental model and will trigger unintended actions.

rule.statement: Choose one term per concept and enforce it across all UI text, documentation, and support content — no synonyms in the same product.
rule.rationale: Using "Create" on one screen and "Add" on another makes users wonder if they are different operations. One term per concept eliminates that doubt.

rule.statement: If any Applies-If precondition fails OR any Skip-If condition triggers, do NOT apply this methodology. Emit a skip-record naming the failed precondition / triggered skip, and route the task to the correct methodology (or none).
rule.rationale: Methodology hygiene: mis-application produces worse artefacts than no methodology because downstream consumers trust the schema; the skip-record makes non-application traceable.
